introduction_markdown:
Multiple choice paper (0780 Physics 1, June 2023, Advanced Level, one and a half hours). Answer ALL 50 questions; all questions carry equal marks. Each question has FOUR suggested answers A, B, C and D; mark only one answer for each question (if you mark more than one you score zero). Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room. The use of a calculator and the Formulae book is allowed.

**Constants used in the answers** (the paper itself prints no data sheet): acceleration of free fall $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ (question 14 uses the value $10\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$ given in its text); specific heat capacity of water $4200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$; specific latent heat of vaporisation of water $2.26\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$; speed of light $c = 3.00\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; Planck constant $h = 6.63\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**Section I (thirty five questions), Questions 1-35.** Directions: Each of the thirty five questions or incomplete statements in this section is followed by four suggested answers. Select the best answer in each case.

**Section II (ten questions), Multiple Selection, Questions 36-45.** Directions: for each group of questions below ONE or TWO of the responses given is/are correct. Then choose: A - if 1 and 2 are correct; B - if 2 and 3 are correct; C - if 1 only is correct; D - if 3 only is correct. (Directions summarised: A = 1, 2 only; B = 2, 3 only; C = 1 only; D = 3 only.)

**Section III (five questions), Questions 46-50.** Directions: Each of the questions (46-50) has four sets of graphs A-D. Which of the graphs in each question best fits the relationship between $x$ and $y$.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following consists of only scalar quantities?
questions.corrige_markdown: A scalar has magnitude only; a vector also has a direction. Electric field intensity (option A), momentum, acceleration and displacement (B) and electromagnetic force (D) are vectors. Charge, work (energy transferred) and temperature are all scalars. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: Electric field intensity, mass, and volume

questions.enonce_markdown: Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiments reveal strongly that an atom
questions.corrige_markdown: Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil, a few were deflected through large angles and about one in $10^4$ was turned back through more than $90^\circ$. Large deflections need a strong repulsive force from a very small region holding all the positive charge and nearly all the mass: a nucleus of tiny size ($\sim 10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m}$ against $\sim 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$ for the atom) and very high density. Options B and D describe the plum-pudding model, which the experiment disproved. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: Has a nucleus of very small size and very high density.
has a nucleus of relatively large size and of low density
is a positive mass with electrons spreading all over inside to make it neutral

questions.enonce_markdown:
A ball bearing was made to fall freely through a viscous liquid in a very long tube. State which of the following statements is true?

*Options as printed:* A) The acceleration of the ball remains constant throughout.   B) The net upward force remains constant.   C) The net downward force remains constant.   D) The velocity of the ball remains constant throughout
questions.corrige_markdown:
Three forces act on the ball: its weight $W$ downwards, the upthrust $U$ upwards and the viscous drag $F_v$ upwards. $F_v$ grows with the speed. At the start $F_v=0$ and the net downward force is $W-U$; as the ball speeds up $F_v$ increases, so the net downward force $W-U-F_v$ and the acceleration $a=(W-U-F_v)/m$ both decrease; when $F_v=W-U$ the net force and the acceleration are zero and the ball falls at constant terminal velocity (reached because the tube is very long).

Therefore the acceleration (A) and the net downward force (C) decrease from their initial values to zero and are not constant, and the speed (D) only becomes constant once terminal velocity is reached, not "throughout". Option B (a constant net upward force) is false as well. Statement D is the only one that becomes true, and only after a long time, so no option is true as worded and no letter is designated.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the force diagram(s) show(s) an object moving to the right with a constant velocity?

![fig-1](gce-al-physics-2023-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

*Options as printed:* the diagrams A to D of the figure (A: 25 N up, 25 N down, 20 N left, 20 N right; B: the same as A with a duplicated 25 N label; C: 25 N up and 25 N down only; D: 25 N up, 25 N down and 20 N to the right).
questions.corrige_markdown:
Constant velocity means zero resultant force (Newton's first law), and the diagrams do not show the direction of motion, so the test is only whether the forces balance.

- **A:** vertical forces $25\ \mathrm{N}$ up and $25\ \mathrm{N}$ down balance; horizontal forces $20\ \mathrm{N}$ left and $20\ \mathrm{N}$ right balance. Resultant $=0$.
- **B:** drawn like A, with an extra duplicated "25 N" label next to the upward arrow. Vertical $25\ \mathrm{N}$ up and down, horizontal $20\ \mathrm{N}$ left and right: resultant $=0$ (if the extra label is only a printing defect).
- **C:** only $25\ \mathrm{N}$ up and $25\ \mathrm{N}$ down, no horizontal force. Resultant $=0$: an object with no horizontal force keeps its horizontal velocity, so it can move to the right at constant velocity.
- **D:** a single horizontal force of $20\ \mathrm{N}$ to the right is unbalanced, so the object accelerates to the right. Not constant velocity.

Three diagrams (A, B and C) have a zero resultant force, but the question expects a single answer, so the question is ambiguous and no letter is designated.

questions.enonce_markdown: According to Newton's third law, every force is accompanied by an equal and opposite reaction force. The reason why these forces do not cancel each other is?
questions.corrige_markdown: The action and reaction forces of Newton's third law are always equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, act for the same time and are of the same kind, but they act on two different bodies. Forces cancel only when they act on the same body, so the pair never produces a zero resultant on one object. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: the action force acts for a longer time period
the two forces are not always in the same direction
one of the two forces is greater than the other
the two forces act upon different objects; only forces on the same object can balance each other.

questions.enonce_markdown: A student applies a force of $26\ \mathrm{N}$, parallel to a plane surface inclined at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal in order to pull an object of weight $40\ \mathrm{N}$ along the plane surface at constant speed. The frictional force between the plane and the object is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The object is pulled up the slope at constant speed, so the forces along the plane balance. The component of the weight down the slope is $W\sin 30^\circ = 40\times 0.5 = 20\ \mathrm{N}$. Down the slope act this component and the friction $f$; up the slope acts the pull of $26\ \mathrm{N}$:
$$26 = 20 + f \;\Rightarrow\; f = 6\ \mathrm{N}.$$
The pull is not equal to the friction (option C) because part of it supports the weight component. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 2 shows a transverse wave travelling through a medium to the right. See diagram below. The particles of the medium are vibrating.

![fig-2](gce-al-physics-2023-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)
questions.corrige_markdown: In a transverse wave each particle oscillates at right angles to the direction in which the wave travels. The wave travels along CI (the equilibrium line), and the line AD joins the crest A to the point D directly below it on CI, so AD is perpendicular to CI. The particles therefore vibrate parallel to AD. Motion along CI (option C) would be a longitudinal wave. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: perpendicular to the line joining AD.
parallel to the line joining AD.
at various angles to the line CI.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following statements is true concerning a ball thrown vertically upwards and caught on its return by the thrower?
questions.corrige_markdown: Taking air resistance as negligible (the question does not mention it), the only force on the ball after release is its weight, so its acceleration is $g=9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ downwards at every instant, going up, at the top and coming down: constant. The speed (B) decreases to zero at the top and then increases, and the velocity (C) changes in magnitude and direction. The times up and down are equal by symmetry (A). (With significant air drag the upward trip would be shorter, but the standard idealisation is intended.) **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: the ball takes a shorter time to go up than to come down.
the speed is constant throughout the flight.
the velocity is constant throughout the flight
the acceleration is constant throughout the flight.

questions.enonce_markdown: A power cable carrying a current of $300\ \mathrm{A}$ is placed normally in a uniform B-field of flux density $10^{-5}\ \mathrm{T}$. If the cable experiences a force of $1.2\ \mathrm{N}$, then the length of the cable is
questions.corrige_markdown:
For a conductor at right angles to the field, $F = BIL$. So
$$L = \frac{F}{BI} = \frac{1.2}{10^{-5}\times 300} = \frac{1.2}{3\times 10^{-3}} = 400\ \mathrm{m}.$$ **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which thermometer is best for measuring rapidly changing temperatures?
questions.corrige_markdown: A thermometer follows a rapid change only if it has a very small thermal capacity, so that it reaches the new temperature almost immediately. The thermocouple junction is tiny, with a very small heat capacity, and it gives an e.m.f. that responds almost instantly. The liquid-in-glass bulb, the gas bulb and the platinum coil have larger thermal capacities and respond slowly. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The amount of energy needed to completely convert $1\ \mathrm{kg}$ of pure water at $60\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to steam at $100\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and at atmospheric pressure is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Two stages are needed (the paper prints no data; the usual values $c_\mathrm{water}=4200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ and $l_v=2.26\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$ are used, the latter being the figure in option B):

1. Heating the water from $60\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $100\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$: $Q_1 = mc\Delta\theta = 1\times 4200\times 40 = 1.68\times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{J}$.
2. Boiling at $100\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$: $Q_2 = ml_v = 1\times 2.26\times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{J}$.

Total $Q=Q_1+Q_2 = 2.428\times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{J}\approx 2.43\times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{J}$. Options A and B each give only one stage. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 3 shows three charges of the same sign and magnitude placed at points R, S and T. The point at which the resultant electric field strength is zero is:

![fig-3](gce-al-physics-2023-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)

*Options as printed:* A) Between R and S   B) Midway between S and T   C) Between S and T but closer to T   D) Lies along the line joining R and T but behind T or B
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let each charge be $q$ (same sign), with R, S, T in that order along a line.

- **Outside the segment RT** (behind R or behind T) all three fields point the same way (away from the charges), so the resultant cannot be zero. Option D is false.
- **Between S and T:** the fields of R and S point towards T and the field of T points towards S. Close to S the field of S is very large and points towards T; close to T the field of T is very large and points towards S. The resultant therefore changes sign between S and T, so there is a point of zero field there. Because the fields of R and S both push towards T, the zero lies closer to T than the midpoint (option C true, option B false). For equal spacing $d$ the zero is at $0.514\,d$ from S.
- **Between R and S:** the field of R points towards S, the fields of S and T point towards R. Close to R the field of R dominates and close to S the field of S dominates, in opposite directions, so the resultant also changes sign and a second point of zero field exists between R and S (option A also true). For equal spacing it is $0.514\,d$ from R, i.e. closer to S.

A system of three like charges on a line always has two such points, so options A and C are both correct and the question has no single key; no letter is designated.

questions.enonce_markdown: A light ray which is incident on an air - water boundary at an angle of incidence different from zero. Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.corrige_markdown: Snell's law states that $\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}=n$, a constant for the two media (here $n\approx 1.33$ for air to water). In water the speed of light decreases ($v=c/n$) and the wavelength decreases ($\lambda=v/f$) while the frequency, fixed by the source, does not change. So B, C and D are false. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is constant.
The wavelength of the light increases as it moves from air to water.
The speed of light increases as it moves from air to water.
The frequency of light increases as it moves from air to water.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The force on a $1\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass on the surface of the earth is $10\ \mathrm{N}$. If the radius of the earth is $6400\ \mathrm{km}$, the force on $91\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass at a point $4000\ \mathrm{km}$ from the centre of the earth (assume the earth has uniform density) is

*Options as printed:* A) $1.6\ \mathrm{N}$   B) $67.6\ \mathrm{N}$   C) $16.0\ \mathrm{N}$   D) $6.3\ \mathrm{N}$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Inside a uniform sphere the field strength is proportional to the distance from the centre: $g_r = g\dfrac{r}{R}$. So
$$g_r = 10\times\frac{4000}{6400} = 6.25\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}.$$
For the $91\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass printed in the question, $F = 91\times 6.25 = 568.75\ \mathrm{N}\approx 569\ \mathrm{N}$, and this value is not among the options. The options are of the size expected for a mass of $1\ \mathrm{kg}$ (force $6.25\ \mathrm{N}\approx 6.3\ \mathrm{N}$, option D), so "91 kg" is probably a misprint for "1 kg". Option C ($16.0\ \mathrm{N}$) comes from inverting the ratio ($10\times 6400/4000$). Because the printed data and the options do not agree, no letter is designated.

questions.enonce_markdown: An a.c signal of $400\ \mathrm{Hz}$ is applied to the y-plate of a CRO whose time-base is set at $2\ \mathrm{ms\,cm^{-1}}$. The number of cycles on the $60\ \mathrm{cm}$ wide screen of the CRO is
questions.corrige_markdown: Period of the signal: $T = \dfrac{1}{f}=\dfrac{1}{400}=2.5\ \mathrm{ms}$. At $2\ \mathrm{ms\,cm^{-1}}$ one cycle occupies $\dfrac{2.5}{2}=1.25\ \mathrm{cm}$ of the screen. Number of cycles on $60\ \mathrm{cm}$: $\dfrac{60}{1.25}=48$. (Equivalently the trace lasts $60\times 2=120\ \mathrm{ms}$ and $400\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\times 0.120\ \mathrm{s}=48$.) **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A train of mass $m$ is travelling with a speed $v$. If the mass of the train is tripled by loading it, and if the velocity is halved, then how will the kinetic energy of the train vary?
questions.corrige_markdown: Initially $E_k=\tfrac12 mv^2$. Finally $E_k'=\tfrac12 (3m)\left(\tfrac v2\right)^2=\tfrac38 mv^2=\tfrac34\left(\tfrac12 mv^2\right)$. The new kinetic energy is $\tfrac34$ of the original, that is the energy is multiplied by $\tfrac34$ (it decreases). Option A is the only one that matches (read as "decreases to 3/4 of its value"). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 4 shows an electric circuit. The reading on V is

![fig-4](gce-al-physics-2023-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_4.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The two branches are in parallel across the $6\ \mathrm{V}$ cell (cell resistance neglected, voltmeter ideal).

- Left branch: $3+1=4\ \Omega$, $I=\dfrac64=1.5\ \mathrm{A}$. Taking the lower rail as $0\ \mathrm{V}$, the mid-point is at $V=1.5\times 1=1.5\ \mathrm{V}$.
- Right branch: $4+6=10\ \Omega$, $I=\dfrac{6}{10}=0.6\ \mathrm{A}$, the mid-point is at $V=0.6\times 6=3.6\ \mathrm{V}$.

The voltmeter reads the potential difference between the mid-points: $3.6-1.5=2.1\ \mathrm{V}$. Options A and C are single p.d.s, and D is their sum. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A vehicle is climbing a hill at constant velocity. Which of the following statements about the vehicle is true?
questions.corrige_markdown: Constant velocity means zero acceleration and so zero resultant force. By Newton's second law $F_\mathrm{net}=\dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$, so the rate of change of momentum is zero (A). The net force is zero, not upward (B). Friction at the driving tyres is needed to move the car (C false). The driving force must balance both the friction and the component of the weight down the slope, so it is larger than the friction alone (D false). **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: The rate of change of the vehicle's momentum is zero.
The net force acting on the vehicle is pointing upwards.
The frictional force between the vehicle and the surface is zero.
The force produced by the vehicle's engine is equal to the frictional force between the tyres and the road.

questions.enonce_markdown: A stretched string is made to vibrate such that its third harmonic frequency is $2000\ \mathrm{Hz}$. Its fundamental frequency is
questions.corrige_markdown: For a string fixed at both ends the $n$th harmonic has frequency $f_n=nf_1$. So $f_1=\dfrac{f_3}{3}=\dfrac{2000}{3}=667\ \mathrm{Hz}$ (666.7 Hz). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A pure inductor has an inductance of $5\times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{H}$. Calculate the rate of change of current through it that would produce an induced emf of $100\ \mathrm{V}$.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The magnitude of the induced emf in an inductor is $\varepsilon=L\left|\dfrac{dI}{dt}\right|$. So
$$\frac{dI}{dt}=\frac{\varepsilon}{L}=\frac{100}{5\times10^{-2}}=2000\ \mathrm{A\,s^{-1}}.$$ **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The pressure $P$, volume $V$ and temperature of a real gas are related by the equation $\left(P+\dfrac{a}{V^2}\right)(V-b)=RT$, the unit of the constant, "$a$" is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Quantities added together must have the same unit, so $\dfrac{a}{V^2}$ has the unit of pressure: $[a]=[P][V^2]$. Pressure is force per area: $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$ and $[V^2]=\mathrm{m^{6}}$. Hence
$$[a]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}\times \mathrm{m^{6}}=\mathrm{kg\,m^{5}\,s^{-2}}.$$
Option A is the unit of pressure itself. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A body, $x$, of mass, $m$, moving with a velocity, $v$, makes an elastic head on collision with a stationary body, $y$, of same mass, $m$. Which of the following combinations correctly describes the velocities of $x$ and $y$ after collision.
questions.corrige_markdown: Let the final velocities be $v_x$ and $v_y$. Momentum: $mv=mv_x+mv_y\Rightarrow v=v_x+v_y$. An elastic collision also conserves kinetic energy: $v^2=v_x^2+v_y^2$. Squaring the first equation and comparing gives $2v_xv_y=0$, so $v_x=0$, $v_y=v$ (the other solution $v_x=v$, $v_y=0$ means no collision). The bodies exchange velocities. Option C conserves momentum but loses half of the kinetic energy (perfectly inelastic collision), and D does not conserve momentum. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The half life of a radioactive isotope, X, is $10$ hours. If the original activity is $20\ \mathrm{Bq}$, its activity in Bq, after $30$ hours will be
questions.corrige_markdown: $30\ \mathrm{h}$ is $\dfrac{30}{10}=3$ half-lives, so $A=A_0\left(\tfrac12\right)^3=\dfrac{20}{8}=2.5\ \mathrm{Bq}$ ($20\to10\to5\to2.5$). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A battery of emf $10\ \mathrm{V}$ and internal resistance $3$ ohms is connected to a resistor. If the current in the circuit is $0.5\ \mathrm{A}$, what is the resistance of the resistor and the p.d. across it when the circuit is closed?
questions.corrige_markdown: p.d. across the resistor (terminal p.d.): $V=E-Ir=10-0.5\times3=8.5\ \mathrm{V}$. Resistance: $R=\dfrac{V}{I}=\dfrac{8.5}{0.5}=17\ \Omega$ (check: $E=I(R+r)\Rightarrow R=\dfrac{10}{0.5}-3=17\ \Omega$). Option B gives the total resistance $20\ \Omega$ and the e.m.f. instead. (Options C and D are printed identically.) **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: When a forward bias p.d is applied to a p-n junction, it;
questions.corrige_markdown: In forward bias the p side is made positive with respect to the n side. The external p.d. opposes the built-in junction (barrier) potential, so the barrier is lowered and the depletion layer narrows. As a consequence more majority carriers cross the junction (D) and the forward current rises (C is false, the majority-carrier current increases). Raising the barrier (B) describes reverse bias. Option A states the direct effect of the bias, while D is a result of it, so A is the best answer. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: increase number of carriers crossing the junction

questions.enonce_markdown:
A silver wire has a resistance of $2.1$ ohms at $27.5\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and a resistance of $2.7$ ohms at $100\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The temperature coefficient of the silver wire is?

*Options as printed:* A) $0.02\ ^\circ\mathrm{C^{-1}}$   B) $0.05\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$   C) $0.005\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$   D) $0.009\ ^\circ\mathrm{C^{-1}}$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The temperature coefficient of resistance is the fractional change of resistance per degree. Using the resistance at $27.5\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ as the reference:
$$\alpha=\frac{R_2-R_1}{R_1\,\Delta\theta}=\frac{2.7-2.1}{2.1\times(100-27.5)}=\frac{0.6}{152.25}=3.9\times10^{-3}\ ^\circ\mathrm{C^{-1}}.$$
If instead $R_\theta=R_0(1+\alpha\theta)$ with $R_0$ the resistance at $0\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$, then $\dfrac{2.7}{2.1}=\dfrac{1+100\alpha}{1+27.5\alpha}$ gives $\alpha=4.4\times10^{-3}\ ^\circ\mathrm{C^{-1}}$. Both values are close to the true value for silver (about $4\times10^{-3}\ ^\circ\mathrm{C^{-1}}$), and neither matches an option: A is five times too large, B and C have the wrong unit, and D ($0.009$) is near the slope $\dfrac{0.6}{72.5}=0.0083\ \Omega\,^\circ\mathrm{C^{-1}}$, which is not a temperature coefficient. The printed options are faulty, so no letter is designated.

questions.enonce_markdown: A $10\ \mathrm{kW}$ drilling machine is used to drill a hole in an aluminium block of mass $8.0\ \mathrm{kg}$. How much is the rise in temperature of the block in $2.5$ minutes, given that the specific heat capacity of aluminum is $910\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Assume all the energy delivered goes into heating the block. Time: $2.5\ \mathrm{min}=150\ \mathrm{s}$. Energy: $E=Pt=10\,000\times150=1.5\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{J}$. Then $E=mc\Delta\theta$:
$$\Delta\theta=\frac{1.5\times10^{6}}{8.0\times910}=206\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}.$$ **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 5 shows a potentiometer the test cell of emf $1.5\ \mathrm{V}$ is balanced at the point C. What is the p.d between the ends A and B of the potentiometer?

![fig-5](gce-al-physics-2023-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_5.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The wire is uniform, so the p.d. along it is proportional to length. At balance the p.d. across $AC=60\ \mathrm{cm}$ equals the e.m.f. of the test cell, $1.5\ \mathrm{V}$: the p.d. per unit length is $k=\dfrac{1.5}{60}=0.025\ \mathrm{V\,cm^{-1}}$. For the whole wire $AB=100\ \mathrm{cm}$:
$$V_{AB}=0.025\times100=2.5\ \mathrm{V}.$$
This is less than the $4\ \mathrm{V}$ of the driver cell, as it must be since the rheostat takes some of the p.d. Option B comes from using $40\ \mathrm{cm}$ instead of $60\ \mathrm{cm}$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following quantities has units?
questions.corrige_markdown: A relative quantity that is a ratio of two like quantities has no unit. The relative refractive index ($n=c_1/c_2$, ratio of speeds) and the relative permeability ($\mu_r=\mu/\mu_0$) are pure numbers. The relative velocity is the velocity of one body measured from another, so it is a velocity with unit $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (Options C and D are printed identically, probably a misprint for permeability and permittivity, both dimensionless.) **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 6 shows an electric circuit which contains two resistors and two sources of emf. The internal resistances of the batteries are negligible. Which of the following is correct?

![fig-6](gce-al-physics-2023-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_6.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the figure both cells have their longer (positive) plate on the right, so they drive current in opposite senses around the loop and oppose each other. The net e.m.f. is $12-4=8\ \mathrm{V}$ (in the sense of the $12\ \mathrm{V}$ cell). Total resistance $6+10=16\ \Omega$. Current:
$$I=\frac{8}{16}=0.5\ \mathrm{A}.$$
Then $P_{R_1}=I^2R_1=0.25\times6=1.5\ \mathrm{W}$ (A true); $V_{R_2}=IR_2=5\ \mathrm{V}$ (B false); $I=0.5\ \mathrm{A}$, not $1.0\ \mathrm{A}$ (C false, this value comes from wrongly adding the e.m.f.s: $16/16$); $P_{R_2}=0.25\times10=2.5\ \mathrm{W}$ (D false). **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: The current in the circuit is $1.0\ \mathrm{A}$

questions.enonce_markdown: A simple harmonic oscillator has a period of $0.01\ \mathrm{s}$ and amplitude of $0.2\ \mathrm{m}$. The maximum velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ of the oscillation is
questions.corrige_markdown:
For simple harmonic motion $v_\mathrm{max}=\omega A$ with $\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{T}$:
$$v_\mathrm{max}=\frac{2\pi}{0.01}\times0.2=125.7\approx126\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}.$$
Option B ($62.8$) is obtained by using $\pi$ instead of $2\pi$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A mass of $50\ \mathrm{g}$ is attached to a spring which is fixed at supports, A and C as shown in figure 7. The tension in AB is

![fig-7](gce-al-physics-2023-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_7.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The knot B is in equilibrium under three forces: the weight $W=mg$ downwards, the horizontal tension in BC, and the tension $T$ in AB acting along the string, which makes $30^\circ$ with the vertical. With $g=9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ (not printed on the paper): $W=0.050\times9.81=0.4905\ \mathrm{N}$. Vertical components: $T\cos30^\circ=W$,
$$T=\frac{0.4905}{\cos30^\circ}=\frac{0.4905}{0.866}=0.566\approx0.57\ \mathrm{N}.$$
(The horizontal component gives $T_{BC}=T\sin30^\circ=0.28\ \mathrm{N}$.) The other options come from wrong angles: $W/\sin30^\circ=0.98\ \mathrm{N}$ (A), $W\sin30^\circ=0.25\ \mathrm{N}$ (B), $W\cos30^\circ=0.42\ \mathrm{N}$ (C). **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 8 shows a straight wire passing through a piece of cardboard. The wire carries a current $I$. Which of the following is correct about the direction of the magnetic field formed?

![fig-8](gce-al-physics-2023-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_8.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the figure the positive terminal of the cell is at the top, so the conventional current flows up the right side, along the top and down the wire through the card (the arrow $I$ points downwards). The field lines are circles around the wire. By Maxwell's corkscrew (right-hand screw) rule, turning a right-handed screw so that it advances in the direction of the current gives the direction of the field: for a current going away from an observer looking down from above, the field is clockwise.

The other options quote laws that do not give the field direction of a steady current: Lenz's law gives the direction of an induced current, Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction of the force on a current in a field, and Fleming's right-hand rule gives the direction of an induced current. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: It is clockwise as given by Lenz's law
It is anti-clockwise according to Fleming's left-hand rule
It is anti-clockwise according to Fleming's right-hand rule
It is clockwise according to Maxwell's corkscrew rule

questions.enonce_markdown:
The table below shows four energy levels of the hydrogen atom with their associated energies.

| N | Energy / $10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$ |
|---|---|
| 1 | $-21.8$ |
| 2 | $-5.3$ |
| 3 | $-2.4$ |
| 4 | $-1.3$ |

The shortest wavelength line seen in the emission spectrum of hydrogen can result from a transition between which of these energy levels?
questions.corrige_markdown: The photon wavelength is $\lambda=\dfrac{hc}{\Delta E}$, so the shortest wavelength corresponds to the largest energy drop $\Delta E$. Energy differences (in $10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$): $4\to3$: $1.1$; $3\to1$: $19.4$; $4\to1$: $20.5$; $2\to1$: $16.5$. The largest is $4\to1$, with $\lambda=\dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^{8}}{20.5\times10^{-19}}\approx9.7\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{m}$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The pressure of a fixed mass of an ideal gas is doubled by heating at constant volume. Which of the following is true about the gas?
questions.corrige_markdown: At constant volume and fixed mass, $p\propto T$ (pressure law), so the kelvin temperature doubles. The mean kinetic energy per molecule is proportional to $T$, so $\overline{c^2}$ doubles (C true), and the r.m.s. speed $\sqrt{\overline{c^2}}$ increases only by a factor $\sqrt2$ (D false). The mass and the volume are unchanged, so the density (A) and the number of molecules per unit volume (B) are unchanged. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: The density of the gas doubles.
The number of molecules per unit volume doubles.
The mean square speed of the molecules doubles.
The root mean square speed of the molecules doubles

questions.enonce_markdown:
An object is released from an aeroplane travelling horizontally at a height of $200\ \mathrm{m}$ above the ground. Which of the following statements is/are correct?

1. The initial velocity of the object relative to the plane is zero
2. The minimum time taken before the object hits the ground is $6.4\ \mathrm{s}$
3. The horizontal velocity of the object increases with time

*Options as printed:* A) 1 and 2 are correct   B) 2 and 3 are correct   C) 1 only is correct   D) 3 only is correct
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Statement 1 is correct:** at the instant of release the object has the same velocity as the plane, so relative to the plane its velocity is zero.

**Statement 2 is correct:** the vertical motion starts from zero vertical velocity, so $h=\tfrac12gt^2$ and $t=\sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2\times200}{9.81}}=6.4\ \mathrm{s}$ (taking $g=9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, not printed on the paper). Air resistance could only lengthen the fall, so $6.4\ \mathrm{s}$ is the minimum time.

**Statement 3 is false:** with no horizontal force the horizontal velocity stays constant (air resistance would only reduce it).

**Intended answer: A (1 and 2 are correct).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following observations of the photoelectric effect can be explained using the classical wave theory?

1. No time lapse between illumination and emission of electrons
2. Emission only occurs when the frequency of the light is above a certain threshold.
3. Number of emitted electrons per unit time is directly proportional to the light intensity
questions.corrige_markdown:
**1 cannot be explained:** wave theory predicts that an electron needs time to absorb enough energy from the spread-out wave (a delay, longer for dim light), but emission is instantaneous.

**2 cannot be explained:** wave theory predicts emission at any frequency if the intensity is high enough or the light shines long enough, whereas a threshold frequency is observed.

**3 can be explained:** a more intense wave carries more energy per second to the surface, so more electrons are released per second, in direct proportion to the intensity (this is also what the photon model predicts). **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
In the S.I system of units, the unit of current, the ampere, is defined in terms of the force between two parallel conductors placed $1\ \mathrm{m}$ apart in a vacuum. Which of the following statements is/are true?

1. The magnitude of the force doubles if the current through each wire is doubled.
2. When a material of higher permeability is introduced into the space between the wires, the force increases slightly
3. The force acting per unit length of each wire is $2\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$

*Options as printed:* A) 1 and 2 are correct   B) 2 and 3 are correct   C) 1 only is correct   D) 3 only is correct
questions.corrige_markdown:
The force per unit length between two long parallel wires is $\dfrac{F}{L}=\dfrac{\mu I_1I_2}{2\pi d}$.

**Statement 1 is false:** $F\propto I_1I_2$, so doubling both currents multiplies the force by $2\times2=4$.

**Statement 2 is true:** $F\propto\mu$, so a medium of higher permeability between the wires increases the force.

**Statement 3 is false as printed:** for $I_1=I_2=1\ \mathrm{A}$ and $d=1\ \mathrm{m}$ in vacuum, $\dfrac{F}{L}=\dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi}=\dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}}{2\pi}=2\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, not $2\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$. (The statement also does not say that the currents are $1\ \mathrm{A}$.)

Only statement 2 is correct, and no printed option corresponds to "2 only" (the options are 1 and 2, 2 and 3, 1 only, 3 only). The paper is probably misprinted ($2\times10^{-7}$ intended, which would give "2 and 3"), so no letter is designated.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Two waves of the same wavelength, $\lambda$, constant phase difference and same amplitude are emitted from X and Y, as shown in figure 9 above. At P there is a maximum; at Q a minimum and at R a maximum disturbance. Such an observation may be obtained if

![fig-9](gce-al-physics-2023-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_9.png)

1. $XP = YP$
2. $YQ - XQ = \lambda/2$
3. $YR - XP = \lambda/2$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Maxima occur where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths and minima where it is an odd number of half wavelengths (for sources in phase).

**Statement 1 is correct:** P lies on the axis, on the perpendicular bisector of XY, so $XP=YP$ (path difference zero), giving the central maximum.

**Statement 2 is correct:** Q is the first minimum next to the central maximum, so the path difference is $\lambda/2$: $YQ-XQ=\lambda/2$.

**Statement 3 is false:** R is the next maximum, where the path difference $YR-XR$ must be $\lambda$. As printed, the statement ($YR-XP=\lambda/2$) compares distances to two different points and cannot give a maximum condition at R. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following types of damping would be most suitable for a moving coil galvanometer?

1. critical damping
2. heavy damping
3. light damping
questions.corrige_markdown: A galvanometer pointer should reach its final reading in the shortest time without oscillating. Critical damping does exactly that (the coil returns to equilibrium without overshoot in the shortest time), so statement 1 is correct. Heavy damping makes the pointer creep slowly towards the reading (2 false) and light damping lets it oscillate about the reading before settling (3 false). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which pair(s) of the following statements is/are true about progressive and stationary waves.

| | For progressive waves | For stationary waves |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | There is no net transfer of energy | There is net transfer of energy |
| 2 | Amplitude is constant. | Adjacent points have different Amplitudes |
| 3 | There is gradual phase variation | Points between adjacent nodes are in phase |
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Pair 1 is false:** it is reversed. A progressive wave transfers energy along its direction of travel, while a stationary wave has no net transfer of energy (energy is trapped between the nodes).

**Pair 2 is true:** in a progressive wave every particle has the same amplitude, while in a stationary wave the amplitude varies from zero at the nodes to a maximum at the antinodes.

**Pair 3 is true:** along a progressive wave the phase changes gradually from point to point, whereas in a stationary wave all points between two adjacent nodes oscillate in phase. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Convex and concave lenses are image-forming devices. Which of these statements is/are correct about lenses?

1. For an object placed $20\ \mathrm{cm}$ from a convex lens of focal length $4\ \mathrm{cm}$, the image magnification is $0.25$
2. For a convex lens, if the image is larger than the erect object, then the object distance is less than the focal length.
3. If an object is placed between a concave lens and the principal focus then the image formed is larger than the object.

*Options as printed:* A) 1 and 2 are correct   B) 2 and 3 are correct   C) 1 only is correct   D) 3 only is correct
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Statement 1 is true:** $\dfrac1v=\dfrac1f-\dfrac1u=\dfrac14-\dfrac1{20}=\dfrac15$, so $v=5\ \mathrm{cm}$ and $m=\dfrac vu=\dfrac5{20}=0.25$.

**Statement 3 is false:** a concave lens always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image, wherever the object is.

**Statement 2 is ambiguous:** an enlarged image from a convex lens is obtained in two cases: a virtual, erect image when $u<f$ (magnifying glass), and a real, inverted image when $f<u<2f$. If the statement means "the image is erect and larger than the object" it is true; as worded ("larger than the erect object"), it is not true in general, because a larger real image occurs for $f<u<2f$.

The key is therefore "1 only" (C) on the strict reading and "1 and 2" (A) on the intended reading, so no letter is designated.

questions.enonce_markdown:
If a metal wire of cross-sectional area $A$, has $n$ free electrons per unit volume each having a charge $e$ and moving with a drift velocity $v$, then:

1. The total charge in the wire is $ne$
2. The current per unit area is $nev$
3. The rate of flow of charge is $nevA$
questions.corrige_markdown:
**1 is false:** $n$ is the number per unit volume, so $ne$ is the free charge per unit volume; the charge in a wire of length $L$ is $nALe$.

**2 is true:** in a time $t$ the charge crossing area $A$ is that in a length $vt$, i.e. $nAvt\,e$, so $I=nAve$ and the current per unit area (current density) is $J=\dfrac IA=nev$.

**3 is true:** the rate of flow of charge is the current $I=nevA$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following statements is/are true for a sinusoidal signal of peak voltage $V_0$ and Peak current $I_0$ flowing through a capacitor?

1. Average power dissipated through a resistive load is constant.
2. Current always leads voltage by $\pi/2$
3. The average power dissipated in a resistive load is $P_{av}=\dfrac{V_0I_0}{\sqrt2}$
questions.corrige_markdown:
**1 is true:** in a resistive load the instantaneous power $VI=V_0I_0\sin^2\omega t$ oscillates, but its average over a cycle is a constant, $\tfrac12V_0I_0$, the same every cycle.

**2 is true:** for a capacitor $I=C\dfrac{dV}{dt}=\omega CV_0\cos\omega t$, so the current leads the voltage by $\pi/2$.

**3 is false:** $P_{av}=V_\mathrm{rms}I_\mathrm{rms}=\dfrac{V_0}{\sqrt2}\dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt2}=\dfrac{V_0I_0}{2}$, not $\dfrac{V_0I_0}{\sqrt2}$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
If you dip your hand in alcohol and remove it, it feels cooler than the other fingers because;

1. Alcohol is a good conductor of heat
2. the alcohol is at a lower temperature than the atmospheric temperature
3. the alcohol molecules absorbs energy from the finger as they evaporate
questions.corrige_markdown: Alcohol evaporates quickly. The molecules that escape from the liquid are the most energetic ones, and they take the latent heat of vaporisation from the skin (and from the liquid), so the finger cools: statement 3 is true. Statement 1 is false (liquids such as alcohol are poor conductors, and conduction would not explain the cooling by itself). Statement 2 is false: the alcohol has been standing in the room, so it is at the same temperature as the atmosphere. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The graphs below are for $y$ = average kinetic energy of molecules of a substance undergoing a change of state, and $x$ = temperature of the substance.

![fig-10](gce-al-physics-2023-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_10.png)

*Options as printed:* A) y constant (horizontal line)   B) straight line rising from a positive y-intercept   C) straight line rising from a positive x-intercept   D) vertical line at a fixed value of x
questions.corrige_markdown:
During a change of state (melting, boiling) the temperature of the substance stays constant while the energy supplied increases the potential energy of the molecules. The average kinetic energy of the molecules is proportional to the kelvin temperature, so it is constant as well. Both $x$ and $y$ keep one fixed value, so the "graph" would be a single point.

Graph A (a horizontal line, $y$ constant while $x$ varies) would need the temperature to change, which does not happen. Graph D (a vertical line, $x$ constant while $y$ varies) would need the kinetic energy to change at fixed temperature, which contradicts $\overline{E_k}\propto T$. Graphs B and C show $E_k$ rising with temperature. No graph fits exactly, and both A and D can be argued, so no letter is designated.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The graphs below are for $y$ = maximum kinetic energy of a photoelectron, and $x$ = frequency of incident radiation.

![fig-11](gce-al-physics-2023-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_11.png)
questions.corrige_markdown: Einstein's photoelectric equation: $E_{k,\max}=hf-\phi$, a straight line of gradient $h$. There is no emission (and so $E_{k,\max}=0$) below the threshold frequency $f_0=\phi/h$, so the line cuts the $x$-axis at $f_0>0$ and does not pass through the origin. This is graph C (a rising straight line with a positive intercept on the $x$-axis). Graph B has a positive $y$-intercept (kinetic energy even at $f=0$), A is constant and D is vertical. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The graphs below are for $y$ = potential energy of a planet orbiting the sun, and $x$ = distance from the sun.

![fig-12](gce-al-physics-2023-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_12.png)

*Options as printed:* A) y constant (horizontal line)   B) straight line through the origin   C) decreasing curve (hyperbola) approaching a constant   D) rising curve levelling off from the origin
questions.corrige_markdown: The gravitational potential energy of the planet is $E_p=-\dfrac{GMm}{r}$ (zero at infinity). It is negative, becomes more and more negative as $r$ decreases, and increases towards zero as $r$ grows, the curve levelling off at large $r$. The shape of graph D (rising and flattening) matches this trend (up to the position of the axes), whereas graph C (falling with $r$) is the shape of the magnitude $\dfrac{GMm}{r}\propto\dfrac1r$ or of a positive potential energy, which is not the physical result. An examiner may expect C (a $1/r$ curve) or D (the true trend), and neither fits the signed quantity exactly, so no letter is designated.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The graphs below are for $y$ = the magnitude of velocity of a box falling through air from an aeroplane in the sky, and $x$ = the time of fall.

![fig-13](gce-al-physics-2023-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_13.png)

*Options as printed:* A) straight line through the origin   B) rising curve levelling off, starting above zero   C) decreasing curve (hyperbola)   D) rising curve levelling off, starting from the origin
questions.corrige_markdown:
As the box falls, the air resistance grows with speed, so the acceleration decreases and the speed tends to a constant terminal value: the curve rises and levels off (B or D). A straight line through the origin (A) would be free fall without air resistance, and a falling curve (C) is not possible.

The choice between B and D depends on the initial speed. A box dropped from rest starts at zero speed: graph D. A box released from an aeroplane keeps the horizontal velocity of the plane at the start, so the magnitude of its velocity is not zero at $t=0$: graph B (which starts above zero). The data given (aeroplane speed, drag law) do not settle the question, so no letter is designated.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The graphs below are for $y$ = the reactance of a capacitor, and $x$ = frequency of a.c

![fig-14](gce-al-physics-2023-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_14.png)
questions.corrige_markdown: The reactance of a capacitor is $X_C=\dfrac{1}{2\pi fC}\propto\dfrac1f$. The graph is a rectangular hyperbola: $X_C$ is very large at low frequency (infinite for d.c.) and falls towards zero as $f$ increases. This is graph C. A straight line through the origin (B) would be the reactance of an inductor, $X_L=2\pi fL$. **Answer: C.**
